passages.happening:
‘This is Solomon’s Song of Songs’ (verse 1).

Then a woman speaks, full of longing for her beloved. ‘For your love is more delightful than wine’ (verse 2). ‘The fragrance of your perfume is pleasing; your name is like perfume poured out’ (verse 3). She asks him to take her away with him, and a chorus joins her praise (verse 4).

She turns to the women of the city. ‘I am dark, yet lovely, O daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon’ (verse 5). ‘Do not stare because I am dark, for the sun has gazed upon me. My mother’s sons were angry with me; they made me a keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have neglected’ (verse 6).

She asks him where he grazes his flock at noon, so that she need not wander like a veiled woman among the other shepherds (verse 7). He answers, if she does not know, she can follow the tracks of the flock to the shepherds' tents (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The book begins with no narrator and no introductions, only a woman's voice saying what she longs for. This first chapter sets out the book's speakers, the woman, the man, and the women she calls the daughters of Jerusalem, and its two worlds of royal court and countryside.

The small Hebrew word between dark and lovely can mean and or but, so she may be saying dark and lovely or dark but lovely. She means skin darkened by the sun from work outdoors, not her people or race. In the ancient world, as in many places, pale skin went with wealth and leisure, and sun-darkened skin marked someone who labored. Her brothers had made her work the vineyards, so she had no time for her own vineyard, which most readers take as a picture of herself. Kedar was a desert tribe whose tents were woven from black goat hair, and Solomon's curtains were costly. She is both, dark and beautiful, and she says so without apology.

The man is pictured as a king (verse 4) and as a shepherd (verse 7). Many interpreters think these are two ways of seeing the same beloved, as in other ancient love poems. A veiled woman wandering among shepherds might be mistaken for a woman of loose reputation, which is why she wants to know exactly where to find him.
passages.later: Kedar's black tents are known to the psalms: ‘Woe to me that I dwell in Meshech, that I live among the tents of Kedar’ (Psalm 120:5). And the Bible's first word about man and woman stands behind the whole Song: ‘And the man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed’ (Genesis 2:25).
passages.hard:
Why is a book about romantic and physical love in the Bible at all?

The question is old. Early Jewish and Christian readers who valued the Song defended its place by reading it as an allegory of God's love. According to the Mishnah, Rabbi Akiva, in the early second century AD, insisted that it was the holiest of the Writings.

Many modern readers give a different answer. The Song belongs in Scripture because love between a man and a woman is part of the good world God made, and people need wisdom for it as much as for money, speech or work. The Bible does not treat the body as shameful. Genesis 2 ends with the man and woman naked and unashamed. The Song affirms that goodness, and it also sets love within faithfulness, belonging to one person, and patience.

Many readers today hold both answers together. The Song is in the Bible because human love is good, and because human love at its best points to the love of God for his people.
passages.asks: She says she is dark and lovely, and she will not be stared into shame. Ask whether you have let others' eyes tell you that your body, your work or your history is something to hide. And ask what it would mean to receive love, and give it, without shame.

passages.t: Praise for praise, and a house of cedar
passages.happening:
He praises her. ‘I compare you, my darling, to a mare among Pharaoh’s chariots’ (verse 9). ‘Your cheeks are beautiful with ornaments, your neck with strings of jewels’ (verse 10), and he promises ornaments of gold (verse 11).

She answers with her own delight in him, in pictures of fragrance: myrrh, and ‘a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of En-gedi’ (verse 14).

Then they praise each other in matching words. He says, “How beautiful you are, my darling! Oh, how very beautiful! Your eyes are like doves” (verse 15). She replies, “How handsome you are, my beloved! Oh, how delightful! The soft grass is our bed” (verse 16). ‘The beams of our house are cedars; our rafters are fragrant firs’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Comparing a woman to a mare among Pharaoh's chariots was a compliment of beauty and striking presence. Solomon's reign had close ties to Egypt, including horses and chariots brought from there.

Myrrh, nard and henna were luxury perfumes. En-gedi is a real oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea, fed by springs in the desert cliffs, famous in the ancient world for its greenery.

Much of the work of reading the Song is knowing who is speaking. Hebrew marks the gender of many words, so a reader can often tell whether the woman or the man is addressed, though translations that add speaker headings are making careful guesses.

The chapter ends with praise answering praise, how beautiful, how handsome. That pattern of mutual delight runs through the whole book. Their house is the outdoors itself: soft grass for a bed, cedar branches for beams.
passages.later: The Bible remembers Solomon's trade with Egypt: ‘Solomon’s horses were imported from Egypt and Kue’ (1 Kings 10:28). And David hid in the wilderness of En-gedi, the oasis of verse 14 (1 Samuel 24:1).
passages.asks: The lovers answer praise with praise. Ask when you last told someone you love what you find beautiful in them. And ask how you might make a habit of noticing and naming the good in the people closest to you.
